Model Information

Regression transparency

About the regression model

Model version: Balanced Wing Regression v1

Dataset size: 30 passenger aircraft

Regression type: logarithmic power regression

R squared: 0.9762 on logarithmic fuel burn

Adjusted R squared: 0.9735

Leave-one-out estimated error: approximately 9.07%

Weight-only R squared: 0.9708

Aspect ratio/L-D correlation: approximately 0.996

Aspect ratio and estimated maximum lift-to-drag ratio are combined into a balanced wing-quality term Q so the calculator does not count nearly the same aerodynamic information twice.

The score curve is centered at 75 because matching the geometry of a typical modern passenger aircraft already represents a capable engineering design. A score of 90 indicates approximately 10% lower regression-predicted fuel burn than the neutral geometry, while a score of 50 indicates approximately 11% higher predicted fuel burn.

Most of the model's statistical accuracy comes from aircraft weight. The geometry terms explain a smaller portion of the remaining variation and should be interpreted as preliminary relationships rather than proof that changing one feature will directly cause the predicted fuel reduction.

Open the source spreadsheet

Explain it simply

Think of every airplane as racing against a fair opponent that weighs exactly the same amount. This prevents a small airplane from automatically winning just because it burns fewer gallons than a huge airplane. The calculator studies patterns from 30 real aircraft and estimates how weight, wing shape, lift-to-drag ratio, and fuselage shape affect fuel use. A score of 75 means the design matches the neutral comparison airplane, using aspect ratio 9.6, maximum L/D 16.8, and fuselage slenderness 11.2. A score of 90 means its geometry is predicted to use about 10% less fuel, while a score of 50 means about 11% higher predicted fuel burn than neutral. This curve is inspired by the style of math-competition scoring used by organizations such as MAA and tournaments such as SMT and BMT: ordinary performance receives a capable score, while exceptional performance is progressively harder to achieve. It is inspired by those competitions, not copied from an official scoring formula.

Limitations and validity ranges

The source dataset covers approximately MTOW 48,501-1,268,000 lb, aspect ratio 7.527-11.327, estimated maximum L/D 15.40-17.78, and fuselage slenderness 8.567-14.106. Inputs outside those ranges are allowed, but the calculator marks them as extrapolations. For an approximately 180-passenger aircraft, comparisons with similarly sized narrowbody aircraft are more defensible than comparisons spanning everything from regional jets to the A380.

  • Fuel-burn figures in the source sheet are approximate.
  • Real aircraft use different engines, materials, technologies, configurations, routes, speeds, and operating procedures.
  • The historical dataset does not truly hold everything else constant.
  • The formula shows statistical association, not guaranteed causation.
  • Estimated L/D values are not equivalent to wind-tunnel, CFD, or flight-test measurements.
  • The model should not be used for certification, safety decisions, or final engineering design.
  • New designs should eventually be validated using CFD, wind-tunnel testing, physical glide tests, or reliable published aerodynamic data.
